Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Architecture Diagram

The solution contains two catalog web applications, a legacy ASP.NET MVC application and a ported ASP.NET Core application. Both have a catalog service layer and SQL Server persistence mode; the ported application selects mock data by default. A small utilities library is shared between them.

Data Storage & External Services

The legacy application uses SQL Server LocalDB by default. The ported application's UseMockData setting defaults to true; when database mode is enabled, it uses SQL Server LocalDB. Their configured database names are different. The legacy app uses the CatalogDBContext connection in Web.config; the ported app uses DefaultConnection in appsettings.json. Catalog pictures are read from local application files. No external service, message broker, or cache integration was identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The solution contains two parallel catalog implementations with separate EF contexts and data stores.
  • ICatalogService abstracts catalog operations and is registered with either a database-backed or mock implementation.
  • Autofac provides dependency injection; the applications share a binary serialization utility.

DTOs & Contracts

BrandDTO is a service-level response shape used by the files API. CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are service-level domain entities also used by MVC views and API actions. PaginatedItemsViewModel is the catalog list response model. No gateway aggregation DTO, OpenAPI document, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found. BrandDTO is a mutable class; JSON formatting is provided by the application frameworks, while the files endpoint uses the shared binary serializer.

Communication Patterns

  • MVC and API controllers call ICatalogService directly; the service uses EF6 or EF Core, depending on the application.
  • The ported application can register mock catalog data with UseMockData; it does not communicate with another service.
  • No message broker, service discovery, API gateway, retries, circuit breaker, or client-side load balancing was identified.
  • No authentication or authorization middleware is configured. The startup pipeline does not enforce HTTPS; local launch settings advertise HTTP and HTTPS development URLs.
  • The files endpoints return serialized catalog brand data. No client-facing service composition was observed.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports browsing and maintaining an e-commerce product catalog. Users can view products, brands, categories, stock information, and product images through the web applications and their catalog APIs.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogA product offered in the catalog, including price, stock, and image referenceBelongs to one brand and one category
CatalogBrandCatalogA product brandMay be associated with many catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogA product type/categoryMay be associated with many catalog items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server LocalDB or mock data
eShopPortedCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server LocalDB or mock data

Both applications independently implement the same catalog domain. They do not exchange data with each other; each is the source of truth for its own configured store.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse Catalog

  1. A user opens the catalog listing.
  2. CatalogController requests a page of items from ICatalogService.
  3. The service retrieves items and their brand/type data, orders by item identifier, and applies page index and page size.
  4. The controller returns the listing view model.

Workflow 2: Maintain Catalog Item

  1. An operator opens the create or edit form and submits catalog item data.
  2. The controller applies model validation and the explicit model-binding field list.
  3. The service assigns an identifier on creation or updates the existing item.
  4. The service persists the change through Entity Framework; successful operations redirect to the catalog listing.

Workflow 3: Display Product Picture

  1. A client requests a picture using the catalog item identifier.
  2. PicController resolves the catalog item and uses its picture filename to read a local image.
  3. The response is returned with an image media type selected from the filename extension.

Workflow 4: Retrieve Brands

  1. An API client requests the brands collection or one brand by identifier.
  2. The API controller queries ICatalogService and returns the result.
  3. The demo delete action checks for the brand but does not actually remove it.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service API composition, message exchange, or shared database access was found. The legacy and ported applications each read and write their own catalog store. The only common code is the utilities library; it provides binary serialization for a brands response rather than a business-data synchronization flow.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Catalog user" participant Controller as "Catalog controller" participant Service as "Catalog service" participant Context as "Entity Framework context" participant Database as "Catalog database" User->>Controller: Browse catalog with page parameters Controller->>Service: Request catalog page Service->>Context: Count and query catalog items Context->>Database: Read items, brands, and types Database-->>Context: Catalog records Context-->>Service: Page of catalog items Service-->>Controller: Paginated catalog view model Controller-->>User: Render catalog page

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog item name is required; price must be within the configured nonnegative range and have no more than two fractional digits.
  • Stock, restock threshold, and maximum stock values are constrained to nonnegative ranges.
  • Catalog items reference a brand and catalog type; the legacy EF model requires both relationships.
  • List results are ordered by item identifier and paginated using the provided page size and index.
  • The ported application selects mock or database-backed service registration using UseMockData.
  • Create and edit actions persist only model-bound fields and rely on MVC model validation before saving.
  • Brand deletion is a demo-only action and does not mutate data.
  • No authentication, authorization, audit trail, or business-event logging policy was identified.

AppCAT's full package compatibility and vulnerability details are in the versioned report and security assessment.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The solution models a product catalog with three primary entity types. The legacy application uses Entity Framework 6 and the ported application uses Entity Framework Core; both configure SQL Server LocalDB as the default database.

No repository interface separate from ICatalogService was identified. The service classes access their DbContext directly; no custom cache or bulk cross-service lookup method was found.

Caching Strategy

No application cache, distributed cache, second-level ORM cache, or cache-aside strategy was identified. Database-backed catalog reads query Entity Framework directly; mock mode uses in-memory predefined data.

Data Ownership Boundaries

Each web application owns a separate catalog persistence context and uses a different LocalDB database name by default (Microsoft.eShopOnContainers.Services.CatalogDb for the legacy app and eShopPorted for the ported app). No cross-service database access or API-based data composition was found. The mock-data implementations are an alternate local data source rather than a shared data store.
